**BIS finds fintechs far cheaper than banks or stablecoins for cross-border payments**

*Fintechs such as Wise and Remitly cost substantially less than bank wires for cross-border retail payments, while stablecoins continue to suffer from on- and off-ramp friction that limits their competitiveness.*

The Bank for International Settlements has published research comparing the cost and speed of cross-border retail payments across traditional bank channels, fintech providers and stablecoins. The findings show that fintechs such as Wise and Remitly have substantially cut costs relative to bank wires, while stablecoins continue to suffer from friction that limits their competitiveness.

The research provides an empirical baseline against which European policymakers and scheme operators can measure the ambitions of initiatives such as Swift's retail payments scheme, the ECB's cross-currency TIPS pilot and the various stablecoin ventures now seeking European licences. If fintechs already deliver materially cheaper cross-border payments, the case for new infrastructure rests less on cost reduction and more on reach, interoperability or sovereignty.

For banks, the data underlines a competitive gap that regulatory modernisation alone is unlikely to close. Fintechs have built cost advantages through lean operating models and direct FX access, not simply through regulatory arbitrage. Tokenised money remains uncompetitive as a retail remittance solution while on- and off-ramp friction persists, undercutting the case made by stablecoin ventures positioning themselves in this space.

*Sources: [Fintechs top banks and stablecoins for cheap cross-border payment - BIS research](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48630/fintechs-top-banks-and-stablecoins-for-cheap-cross-border-payment---bis-research?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*

**Ninth Wave launches control layer governing AI agent access to bank data**

*A gap that banks and regulators have flagged but no one has yet standardised is now being addressed: how to govern what AI agents can see and do with financial account data.*

Ninth Wave, a US open finance platform that connects financial institutions with third-party applications, has introduced what it calls an Agentic Control Layer, a framework for governing how AI agents access financial account data. The product is designed to give banks and data holders granular controls over AI-initiated data requests, including consent verification, scope limits and audit trails.

The announcement arrives as agentic commerce moves rapidly from concept to production. European banks including ING, Danske Bank and Credit Agricole have completed live agentic payment transactions in recent months, and the Financial Conduct Authority's chief information and digital officer, Jessica Rusu, outlined a framework for agentic finance in a speech on October 19 that envisaged future collaboration between regulators and industry. Yet most of that activity has focused on the payment leg. The data access side, where AI agents query account balances, transaction histories or identity attributes, remains largely ungoverned beyond existing open banking consent frameworks that were designed for human-initiated flows.

Ninth Wave's product is US-focused, but the problem it addresses is universal. European regulators working on PSD3 and open finance legislation will need to decide whether existing strong customer authentication and consent models are adequate when the "customer" initiating access is a software agent acting on a human's behalf.

*Sources: [Ninth Wave launches Agentic Control Layer to govern AI access to bank data](https://app.dealroom.co/news/feed/ninth-wave-launches-agentic-control-layer-to-govern-ai-access-to-bank-data) — Dealroom.co | [Ninth Wave Introduces Agentic Control Layer™ to Govern AI Access to Financial Account Data](https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/ninth-wave-introduces-agentic-control-120000144.html) — Finance | [Ninth Wave Introduces Agentic Control Layer™ to Govern AI Access to Financial Account Data](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261021603767/en/Ninth-Wave-Introduces-Agentic-Control-Layer-to-Govern-AI-Access-to-Financial-Account-Data) — Businesswire*

**Google Cloud outage triggers first real test of EU and UK critical third-party oversight**

*A power failure at a single London data centre disrupted banking services for millions across Europe, prompting the EBA, the FCA and the UK Treasury Committee to demand answers from Google under newly established cloud supervision regimes.*

A power event in Google Cloud's London region on October 20 knocked out digital banking services at Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC for up to eight hours, disabling card payments, transfers and ATM withdrawals for millions of customers. Google attributed the disruption to a fault at a third-party facility in its europe-west2 availability zone and said services had been restored by mid-afternoon.

The European Banking Authority confirmed it had contacted Google Cloud to assess the incident's implications for financial entities across the EU. In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority said it was engaging with Google and affected firms, while Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury Committee, wrote to the Bank of England and FCA seeking details of the regulators' response, the scale of disruption and any financial harm caused. The EBA underlined that designation as a critical third-party provider "does not transfer responsibility for incident management from the provider or relieve financial entities of their own regulatory obligations".

The outage is the first major incident since both regimes came into force. The EU designated 19 technology firms as critical third-party providers under the Digital Operational Resilience Act in 2025, subjecting them to joint oversight by the EBA, ESMA and EIOPA. The UK designated Google Cloud, AWS, Microsoft and Oracle under its own critical third-party regime in July this year. That a single-zone power failure at one provider could simultaneously disable services at four banks underlines the concentration risk both frameworks were designed to address.

*Sources: [Europe's financial regulators query Google over cloud outage that hit banks](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/europes-financial-regulators-query-google-over-cloud-outage-that-hit-banks-4963664) — Reuters via Investing.com*

**Industry panel flags reliability and data gaps as barriers to pay-by-bank growth**

*Executives from Plaid, Barclays, HSBC and Open Banking Limited identified payment success rates and post-payment data as the principal obstacles to scaling account-to-account payments in the UK.*

A panel at Open Banking Expo brought together executives from Plaid, Barclays, HSBC and Open Banking Limited to assess the practical barriers preventing pay-by-bank from competing with cards at scale in the UK. The discussion centred on two persistent problems: payment reliability, where success rates still fall short of card benchmarks, and the data gap after payment initiation, where merchants lack the confirmation and reconciliation information they receive from card networks.

The panel identified commercial variable recurring payments as a key measure of progress under the National Payments Vision, but cautioned that the commercial case for merchants remains difficult to make when reliability is inconsistent across banks and payment corridors. HSBC and Barclays representatives acknowledged that bank-side infrastructure improvements are needed, not just better front-end experiences.

The discussion reflects a tension at the heart of the UK's open banking payments ambitions. The UK Payments Initiative launched in June with GoCardless as its first provider and Moneyhub as its first non-shareholder participant, but scaling beyond early adopters requires solving operational problems that sit with the account-servicing banks rather than with the initiating fintechs.

*Sources: [Open Banking payments face reliability and data barriers, industry warns](https://www.openbankingexpo.com/news/open-banking-payments-must-overcome-reliability-and-data-gaps-to-compete-with-cards-industry-leaders-warn/) — Openbankingexpo*
